paras: The threatened lynching of Goode took place in Appomattox County, Virginia, in August 1900, when a young Black employee on a farm, charged with attempting to assault his employer's wife, was threatened with lynching both during his pursuit and after his trial. When a jury sentenced him to 18 years in the penitentiary rather than death, there were "many threats of lynching," and the court had the sheriff take him to Richmond at once.

Goode, described as "a young negro hardly 15 years of age," was employed on the Appomattox County farm of John Torrence and slept in a room on the upper floor of the house. According to the published account, early one morning while Torrence was away threshing wheat, Goode crept into the room where Mrs. Torrence and her children were asleep on a pallet. The account states that when he attempted to assault her she woke, struck him with her fist and drove him off with a chair.

Goode was pursued at once, and the report says that "had he been captured he would have been lynched." He was later caught in Farmville and tried before a jury in the County Court of Appomattox on about August 10 on the charge of attempting to criminally assault Mrs. Torrence.

The death penalty had been expected, and when the jury returned a verdict of 18 years in the penitentiary there was "much excitement and indignation and many threats of lynching." Because a train was due at Appomattox Station shortly after the verdict, the court, "owing to the state of the public mind," directed the sheriff to take the prisoner to Richmond immediately, and he did so.

The report attributed the jury's leniency to Goode's age, "not quite 15," and to the view that he "did not possess a very bright mind." No attack on the prisoner, arrest of anyone who threatened him, or later follow-up appears in the coverage.

The episode survives in a single unattributed news item, first found in the Alexandria Gazette of August 11, 1900. Six days later the Highland Recorder of Monterey, Virginia, reprinted the same text on its front page under the headline "Young Negro's Crime." Both versions told the story from the accuser's side, calling Mrs. Torrence "a highly respected lady" and the accused "the negro," and reported the threats of lynching that followed a sentence short of death without comment.
No coverage of the case was found in the Black press.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Goode in Appomattox County
bases: A young Black prisoner was pursued by people who, the report says, would have lynched him, and after his conviction 'many threats of lynching' led the court to have the sheriff move him to Richmond (A1); no one was killed.

Goode was not killed: the threats of lynching after the verdict were forestalled when the court had the sheriff take him to Richmond (A1). The episode is a threatened lynching; the size of the group making the threats is not given.
The only two reports found are the same text (A1, reprinted in A2), so there is one account of unstated origin and no independent local, Black-press or court report.

accounts.label: Unattributed Virginia news item
accounts.gist: Goode crept into Mrs. Torrence's room, was beaten off and fled, was pursued and later caught in Farmville; when the jury gave him 18 years instead of death there were many threats of lynching and the court sent him to Richmond.

framing.detail: The Alexandria Gazette ran the item without comment on the threats, presenting the accusation as fact and noting the death penalty 'was expected'.
The Highland Recorder reprinted the item under the headline 'Young Negro's Crime.', treating the charge as an established crime.
